_unitThree: The manuscript never titled its third unit: it types a bare 'UNIT THREE' as the heading and lists it that way in its own hand-typed contents, while units one and two carry their subject ('UNIT ONE: INTRODUCTION TO LITERATURE', 'UNIT TWO - ORAL LITERATURE'). So the contents page showed one untitled unit among three, and the running header on every page of the unit said only 'UNIT THREE'. The subject is not in doubt - the unit opens on written literature and runs through prose, drama and poetry - so give it the same NAME: SUBJECT shape its siblings use. This is the manuscript's own gap, not an engine fault, which is why it is fixed here and not in src/typeset/.
//manuscript-correction: APPLIED DIRECTLY TO THE .docx, and it must be re-applied if that file is ever re-converted from the original. The manuscript bolds every activity label but two - 'Activity 1: In groups, attempt the following riddles?' and 'ACTIVITY: 4 Composing Short Stories' were typed as ordinary body text - so the engine, which starts a callout box on a bold or heading-styled label, did not box them: the riddles label printed as a loose line above its table, and Activity 4 was swallowed into Activity 3's box together with its own four questions. Both runs now carry <w:b/><w:bCs/>, which is all the other 62 labels in the book have. This cannot be done with an override: the box is built at IMPORT time, before overrides run, and the only override that reaches it (boxifyLoose, via boxActivities) rebuilt just one of the two and as a framedsection rather than the exercise box its siblings use. It must not be fixed in src/typeset/ either: a scan of every manuscript in books-to-typeset shows that dropping the bold requirement engine-wide would turn the sentence 'Key points include:' into a Key Points box in Geography For Teachers and newly boxify up to 111 paragraphs in Home Ecnomics Grade 4 TG. A copy of the file as it was is kept beside it as 'LIT in ENG F1 LB.docx.bak-before-bold'. The author should bold both labels in the next issue.
//plot-diagram: Printed page 109's plot diagram (media image19.jpg) was REDRAWN, not upscaled. The manuscript's own bitmap is a screenshot of a third-party graphic: a tiled 'ELEMENTS OF FICTION' watermark runs diagonally across the header about eight times and cuts through the PLOT title, and seven opaque grey rectangles sit on top of the artwork obscuring words in all six definition boxes - Conflict, Exposition, Climax, Rising Action, Falling Action and Resolution. It is greyscale and soft. Upscaling it (which had already been done, to 1625px / 308 DPI) only sharpened the watermark and the grey blocks. Because this is Freytag's pyramid - the diagram Unit Three teaches from, and which the pages after it build on - the page could not be taught from as it stood. The replacement is drawn in TYPST, and its source is kept beside it as 'LIT in ENG F1 LB-art/plot-diagram.typ' so it can be corrected rather than redrawn. It carries the same six element names and the same six definitions, transcribed from the legible parts of the original. No third-party artwork is involved, so there is no licensing question. It is drawn at the width it is PLACED at in the book (134mm, the B5 text column), which is the point of it: an earlier node-canvas attempt was drawn oversized and scaled down, which landed its annotations near 6pt on the page. Rendered at 400 DPI, 2111px across, well over the 300 DPI floor. Nothing here is engine work: it is one book's bad source picture.

blocks.para: **Prose:** written text organised in paragraphs and chapters, for example novels and short stories.
**Drama:** a script meant to be performed on stage, for example plays.
**Poetry:** a piece of writing that uses aesthetic (beautiful) language, arranged in lines and stanzas, for example poems.
In groups, distinguish the three forms of written literature (prose, drama and poetry) and answer the question below.

parts.lead: Every Friday evening, 12-year-old Mwewa and her younger brother Tunde visit their grandmother, Mama Ngozi, who lives in their village. As the family gathers around the cooking fire, Mama Ngozi tells them folktales she heard from her own grandmother stories about clever tortoises, greedy hyenas, brave hunters, and magical rivers. Mwewa loves these evenings because the stories make her laugh, teach her important lessons about honesty and kindness, and help her understand her community’s values. One evening, Mama Ngozi asks Mwewa to retell a story to her cousins, and Mwewa realises that folktales are not just entertaining they are a gift passed down through generations to teach, unite, and inspire.
*Answer the following questions individually in your exercise book.*

parts.q: One Saturday afternoon during the holiday, Nalishebo travelled to the village to visit her grandmother. The village was peaceful and surrounded by green trees, singing birds and fresh air. It was an opportunity for Nalishebo to fully learn the house chores such as sweeping and fetching water from quite a distant place. After helping her grandmother sweep the yard and fetch water from the nearby well, they sat together under a large mango tree to rest. As they enjoyed roasted groundnuts and cool water, grandmother smiled and said, "Today, I will tell you one of the stories my grandmother used to tell me when I was your age."

qseg.t: One Saturday afternoon during the holiday, Nalishebo travelled to the village to visit her grandmother. The village was peaceful and surrounded by green trees, singing birds and fresh air. It was an opportunity for Nalishebo to fully learn the house chores such as sweeping and fetching water from quite a distant place. After helping her grandmother sweep the yard and fetch water from the nearby well, they sat together under a large mango tree to rest. As they enjoyed roasted groundnuts and cool water, grandmother smiled and said, "Today, I will tell you one of the stories my grandmother used to tell me when I was your age."

parts.q: The story was about a clever hare who always used his intelligence to outsmart a greedy hyena. The hyena was selfish and wanted to keep all the food for himself while the hare believed that everyone should have a share. Each time the hyena tried to trick the other animals, the hare found a clever way to teach him a lesson. Nalishebo laughed loudly at the funny tricks the hare played on the hyena. She clapped her hands with excitement whenever the hyena was outwitted. The story entertained her and helped her relax after a busy week of studying at school. When the story ended, Nalishebo eagerly asked her grandmother to tell another one because she was enjoying every moment.

parts.q: As they continued talking, grandmother explained that the story was more than just something to make people laugh. She asked Nalishebo what lessons she had learned from it. Nalishebo replied that she had learned the importance of honesty, kindness and sharing with others. Grandmother nodded and explained that people who are greedy often create problems for themselves just as the hyena did in the story. Nalishebo realised that good behaviour brings peace and happiness while selfishness leads to disappointment.

parts.q: The story also helped Nalishebo learn more about her culture. It included traditional songs that the animals sang during celebrations, village customs that encouraged cooperation and beliefs that had been passed down from one generation to another. As her grandmother sang one of the old songs, Nalishebo happily joined in. She felt proud of her cultural heritage and understood why it was important to preserve such stories for future generations.

parts.q: Some parts of the story made Nalishebo feel sad. She felt sympathy for the smaller animals that were bullied and treated unfairly by the greedy hyena. She admired the hare for standing up for those who could not defend themselves. The story inspired her to be kind, fair and ready to help people who were in need. She promised herself that she would always treat others with respect and never take advantage of anyone.

parts.q: On Monday morning, Nalishebo returned to school full of excitement. During her Literature lesson, the teacher asked the class to share stories they had heard during the weekend. Nalishebo confidently narrated the story of the clever hare and the greedy hyena. Her classmates listened carefully, laughed at the humorous parts and discussed the important lessons they learned from it. Together, they concluded that literature does more than entertain people. It also educates, preserves culture, develops empathy, teaches moral values and helps people understand life and society better.

setMarker.find: Identify and discuss the different elements of drama from above.
Think about characters, setting, and staging.
Who are the characters? What are they doing?
What does the setting look like? Where do you think the play is set?
What do you think the play is about? (Theme)
What is the plot?
Who are the main characters?
What is the main conflict or problem?
What do you think the theme (main message) of the story is?
Now you need to create a simple script. Don’t worry if you’ve never done this before!
Create the Characters: Who are the people in your play? Give them names, and think about what they are like.
Create the Setting: Where and when does your play take place?
Create the Conflict: What is the problem in your play? What are the characters arguing about or struggling with?
Write the Dialogue: Write the conversation between your characters. Make sure it sounds like something people would really say.
Use the Elements: Make sure your script includes some of the elements we discussed in the first activity. For example, can you include a symbol or an element of irony?
After you have your script, it’s time to rehearse.
Decide which group member will play which character.
Practice saying your lines with expression.
Think about where everyone will stand on stage.
Can you use simple props or costumes to make your play more interesting?
